nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
1994 Jan 1. REB|RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution
note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Irish pompano
Scientific Name:  Diapterus auratus (=olisthostomus)

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum:  Chordata
	Class:  Osteichthyes
	Order:  Perciformes
	Family:  Gerreidae

Other Common Names:  Sand perch (1814), silver goatfish

Other:	Reference for Scientific Name (Ranzani 1840).
	Reference for Classification (1914)
	Revision date should be checked

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial: Diapterus auratus is captured with D. plumieri in Indian River Lagoon commercial mojarra fishery (Gilmore pers. obs.).  This fishery has undoubtedly been lumped with the "sand perch" category in  Florida's commercial landings reports (e.g.  2399)
 Recreational:  Occasional landings are reported in the recreational fishery.  Small specimens may be used as bait.
Ecological Role:  In an extensive study of seagrass fish communities in the Indian River Lagoon, Gilmore (1988) found the Irish pompano to be an important component of the fauna.  This species was the most abundant mojarra (Gerreidae; 20,986 individuals) within the Indian River Lagoon seagrass meadows, ranked fifth in overall abundance, ranked second in abundance among non-planktivorous species and was found in over 50% of the 310 collections.  It was also ranked eleventh in biomass and is an epibenthic feeder associated with vegetated and sand/mud benthic habitats.  This species is also important in mangrove communities (2362).
Indicator:  None known.

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Chesapeake Bay to Bahia, Brazil, though absent in the north east Gulf of Mexico (2400; 363; 2146; 2398; Matheson pers. comm.)
Within Study Area:  The Irish pompano is found throughout the Indian River Lagoon system, though is considerably more abundant in the southern portion of the Lagoon (848, 2362; 2320).
Mobility and Migration: Although adults and large juveniles of this principally estuarine (seagrass and mangrove) species can be found in freshwater tributaries, only adults are found around shallow coastal reef formations (848, 1987, 1988).
Life Mode:  The Irish pompano is a euryhaline epibenthic feeder with a wide distribution within the Indian River Lagoon and its freshwater tributaries (1814; 848, 2362, 993, unpub. data;  363).

nodes.title: Habitat Type
nodes.body:
The Irish pompano is found in the Indian River Lagoon from ocean inlets to freshwater tributaries and estuarine wetlands with major collections in seagrass (848, 1988).  Larvae and juveniles from 5 mm have been collected in wetlands fringing the Indian River Lagoon and within seagrass meadows (Gilmore unpub. data).
Substrate:  The Irish pompano is generally found over sand, soft silt/sand or mud bottoms generally near or in association with structure or aquatic vegetation (848; 363; 2320).

nodes.title: Physical/Chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity:  This euryhaline species can occur in salinities ranging from fresh water to 39 ppt (363; 993, unpub. data).
Temperature: tolerance seems to favor a more tropical distribution with cold mortality documented at several locations within the Indian River Lagoon system (1814; 2146; 1888).  Observed temperature range is from 9 to 33.0 C (363; 2146, 993, unpub. data).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode:  The Irish pompano is thought to be gonochoristic, oviparous; eggs fertilized externally (363; Matheson pers. comm.)
Mating/Spawning: Ripe adult females have been taken in Puerto Rico in December and April (363).  Herrema et al. (1985) found adults in breeding condition in April through July and September, however due to limited collections of adults this may not represent the entire spawning season.  A more extended spawning season is indicated as larvae and juveniles less than 20 mm (as small as 5 mm) have been collected in estuarine wetland habitats and seagrass meadows of the Indian River Lagoon from May to December with peaks in abundance in early summer and late fall (Gilmore unpub. data).
Fecundity: No information

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:  Planktonic (Matheson pers. comm.)
Larvae:  Planktonic (Matheson pers. comm.)
Juvenile:  Settle into benthic habitats throughout the Indian River Lagoon at minimum length of 10 mm (993, unpub. data)
Adult:  Irish pompano may reach 30 cm in length (788).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: The gerreid family has mouth morphology specialized for feeding on benthic invertebrates (363; 788).  Austin (1971) reports that the Irish pompano consumes plant material, polychaetes, and pelecypods.

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Due to its great relative abundance, this species is undoubtedly consumed by a variety of predators.  The authors have observed snook predation on this species.
Factors influencing populations:  In an extensive study of seagrass fish communities in the Indian River Lagoon, Gilmore (1988) found the Irish pompano to be an important component of the fauna.  This species was the most abundant mojarra (Gerreidae; 20,986 individuals) within the Indian River Lagoon seagrass meadows, ranked fifth in overall abundance, ranked second in abundance among non-planktivorous species and was found in over 50% of the 310 collections.  It was also ranked eleventh in biomass and is an epibenthic feeder associated with vegetated and sand/mud benthic habitats.  This species is also important in mangrove communities (2362).  Loss of seagrass and estuarine wetland habitat will result in high juvenile mortality in this species.

nodes.title: PEOPLE CONSULTED
nodes.body: Richard E. Matheson, Florida Marine Research Institute, Dept. of Natural Resources, St. Petersburg, Florida.
